summary: The Network Service Header (NSH) has an O bit that marks operations, administration, and maintenance packets, but RFC 8300 left the meaning of "OAM packet" ambiguous. This short document clarifies what is meant and how the bit should be handled. It updates RFC 8300.

eli5.summary: A rulebook had a sign that said "test packet" but nobody agreed what that meant. This note explains it clearly so everyone follows the sign the same way.

questions: what is an oam packet in nsh
what is the nsh o bit
what counts as an nsh oam packet
subtitle: A short fix that pins down what the NSH O bit means: only packets carrying nothing but OAM data count as OAM packets.

tldr.problem: RFC 8300 says the O bit in the Network Service Header marks an OAM packet, but it never said exactly what counts as one, so implementations could disagree on how to treat packets that mix test data with user data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9451 replaces the O bit text in Section 2.2 of RFC 8300. An NSH OAM packet is any NSH-encapsulated packet that exclusively includes SFC OAM data, and packets with user data are not OAM packets. Elements should also discard O-bit packets whose Next Protocol is not itself an OAM protocol.
tldr.outcome: The O bit now has one clear meaning and one clear handling rule. RFC 9451 updates RFC 8300 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9451 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2023. It updates RFC 8300 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Ambiguity Being Fixed
sections.content:
The Network Service Header (NSH), defined in RFC 8300, carries a flag called the O bit that indicates an Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) packet. RFC 8300 left the definition of an OAM packet ambiguous.

RFC 9451 is a short clarification. It replaces the O bit text in Section 2.2 of RFC 8300, and processing of the O bit must follow the updated behavior in its Section 3.
sections.eli5: A flag on a packet meant 'this is a test', but the rules did not say what a test packet really is. This document fills in the gap.

sections.title: Terms the Update Introduces
sections.content:
The document builds on terms from RFC 7665 and RFC 8300 and defines a few more:

  • SFC data plane element: an SFC-aware Service Function (SF), Service Function Forwarder (SFF), SFC Proxy, or Classifier.
  • OAM control element: an NSH-aware element that can generate NSH OAM packets. Any SFC data plane element may behave as one.
  • SFC OAM data: an OAM request (such as Connectivity Verification and Continuity Checks), any data that influences how a companion OAM request runs, the output of an OAM request, or any combination of these.
  • User data: the user packets cited in Section 5.7 of RFC 7665.
sections.eli5: It gives names to the helpers that move packets along and to the two kinds of cargo: test cargo and real user cargo.

sections.title: The New Definition of an NSH OAM Packet
sections.content:
The OLD text called the O bit an OAM packet indicator and left the format and processing outside the scope. The NEW text says that setting the bit indicates an NSH OAM packet: any NSH-encapsulated packet that exclusively includes SFC OAM data. That data can sit in the Fixed-Length Context Header, in optional Context Headers, and in the inner packet.

The O bit is typically set by an OAM controller, or by the final destination of an NSH OAM packet that triggers a response, such as a specific SFC-aware SF or the last SFF of a Service Function Path (SFP). It MUST be set for NSH OAM packets, MUST NOT be set for non-OAM packets, and MUST NOT be modified along the SFP.

NSH-encapsulated packets that include user data are not NSH OAM packets, even if some SFC OAM data (for example, record route) is also in the packet.
sections.eli5: A packet only gets the 'test' flag if it carries nothing but test stuff. If real mail is inside, the flag stays off, even if a little test note is stuck on it.

sections.title: Handling Packets With the O Bit Set
sections.content:
Setting and processing the O bit neither assumes nor expects detailed analysis of any inner IP packet. When SFC OAM data is in the inner packet, the Next Protocol field reflects the structure of that inner OAM packet. To prevent non-deterministic behavior, SFC data plane elements MAY support a configuration parameter that filters valid Next Protocol values in NSH OAM packets.

Absent explicit configuration, SFFs, SFC-aware SFs and SFC Proxies SHOULD discard NSH packets with the O bit set and a Next Protocol that is not itself an OAM protocol. This includes 0x01 (IPv4), 0x02 (IPv6), 0x03 (MPLS) and 0x05 (Ethernet).

An NSH OAM packet MAY include optional Context Headers, such as a subscriber identifier (RFC 8979) or a flow identifier (RFC 9263), to influence how elements process it. It MAY carry SFC OAM data in both Context Headers and the inner packet, and the processing order SHOULD be specified in the relevant OAM or Context Header specification.

Elements that do not support SFC OAM procedures SHOULD discard O-bit packets, but MAY offer a configurable parameter to forward them unmodified. That can be fine for some OAM functions and cause unexpected results for others, so the impact should be analyzed first. The parameter MUST be disabled by default. The actual format and further processing of NSH OAM packets stays outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: If a helper does not know how to handle test packets, it should throw them away by default. It may be told to pass them along, but only if someone has checked that is safe.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The document has no IANA actions. For security, it points to the data plane security and privacy discussion in Section 6 of RFC 7665 and Section 8 of RFC 8300, and to the SFC OAM considerations in Section 9 of RFC 8924.

It adds one requirement: any data included in an NSH OAM packet SHOULD be integrity protected, as described in RFC 9145.
sections.eli5: Test messages can be tampered with like any other, so the data inside them should be sealed so nobody can change it unnoticed.
